title: Humanoid Robots Are Taking Their First Jobs

slides.heading: Humanoid Robots Are Taking Their First Jobs
slides.body: Inside the factories, warehouses, and labs where machines are becoming coworkers

slides.heading: What Is a Humanoid Robot?
slides.body: A humanoid robot has a body shaped like a human — two legs, two arms, and a head. This form factor lets it use the same tools, spaces, and workflows designed for people, without costly redesigns of existing infrastructure.

slides.heading: The Race Is On: Key Players
slides.body: Tesla's Optimus, Figure AI's Figure 02, Boston Dynamics' Atlas, and Agility Robotics' Digit are leading the charge. Major automakers and tech giants have invested billions, signaling this is no longer a research project — it's an industry.

slides.heading: Already on the Factory Floor
slides.body: BMW and Mercedes-Benz have begun piloting humanoid robots for parts handling and assembly tasks. Tesla's Fremont factory now runs Optimus units in internal logistics roles, moving components between stations without human assistance.

slides.heading: How They Learn to Work
slides.body: These robots learn through a combination of reinforcement learning, imitation from human demonstrations, and massive simulation environments. Training in virtual worlds lets a robot accumulate millions of hours of experience before its first real shift.

slides.heading: What Tasks Can They Handle?
slides.body: Current humanoids excel at pick-and-place, sorting, and repetitive material handling. They still struggle with fine manipulation and unpredictable environments — but capabilities are improving rapidly with each new model generation.

slides.heading: The Economics: Why Now?
slides.body: A humanoid robot costs roughly $30,000–$150,000 upfront, compared to $35,000+ per year for a human worker in developed countries. As unit costs fall and uptime reaches 20+ hours a day, the business case is becoming hard to ignore for labor-intensive industries.

slides.heading: Jobs at Risk — and Jobs Created
slides.body: Routine physical jobs in warehousing, manufacturing, and logistics face the highest displacement risk. At the same time, demand is surging for robot trainers, fleet operators, maintenance technicians, and AI safety engineers — roles that didn't exist five years ago.

slides.heading: Safety and Ethical Guardrails
slides.body: Regulators in the EU and US are drafting new workplace safety standards specifically for collaborative humanoid robots. Key debates include liability for accidents, algorithmic bias in task assignment, and mandatory off-switches under human control.

slides.heading: The Coworker of the Future Is Already Here
slides.body: Humanoid robots won't replace human creativity or judgment — but they will transform how physical work gets done. Understanding this shift now puts you ahead of one of the defining technological transitions of the 2020s.
